newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian soldiers search for British hostage.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian soldiers search for British hostage.

text.p: Cambodian government troops were on Sunday trying to establish contact with a group of Khmer Rouge guerrillas and a kidnapped British mine clearance expert believed to be in their company, a senior military officer said.

Major General Tom Sambol said he heard on Saturday that contact had been lost with the guerrillas, who reportedly want to defect, and soldiers had been sent to look for them in the jungles of northern Cambodia.

The general did not elaborate but said General Khan Saveoun, commander of the military region centred round the northwest province of Siem Reap, had flown to Staung district on Sunday to lead the operation.

A top military officer said on Thursday that mine clearance supervisor Christopher Howes and his interpreter Houn Hourth had reached the district's Anlong Kranh village and were expected to arrive in Phnom Penh the following day.

Armed forces deputy chief of staff Lieutenant General Nhiek Bun Chhay said they had escaped from the Anlong Veng base of hardline Khmer Rouge loyal to Pol Pot with the help of their guards and other guerrillas who wanted to defect.

But four days later there has been no confirmation on the freedom of the two men, employees of the Mines Advisory Group of Britain who were abducted by armed men in Siem Reap province on March 26 as they were clearing a rural road of mines.

The British Embassy has stressed that reports of their freedom are premature and there had been no confirmation of their release from the two Scotland Yard police officers sent to the area and in direct contact with the mission.
The embassy has urged caution in reporting but said on Saturday that the Cambodian authorities "give us reports which are cause for hope."

The Khmer Rouge, which ruled Cambodian by terror from 1975-79, has been savaged since August by mass defections. The Maoist movement reneged on a 1991 peace pact and had been fighting the coalition formed after U.N.-run 1993 polls.
